meta.titre: International Trade: exports, exchange rates and terms of trade
meta.sous_theme: Trade between countries, exchange rates and terms of trade

sections.contenu_markdown: Cocoa, timber and crude oil leave Cameroon on ships, while vehicles and machinery arrive in the ports. No country can produce everything it needs at a low cost, so countries trade with one another. International trade also has its own vocabulary: exports, exchange rate, appreciation, dumping, terms of trade. GCE papers ask you to define these terms and to describe a trading relationship, and examiners reward exact definitions.

items: Countries differ in climate, soil, minerals and skills.
Cameroon uses the FCFA, and other countries use other currencies.
Specialisation means concentrating on producing the goods one makes best.

sections.titre: Exports, imports, exchange rates and terms of trade
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What international trade is
International trade is the exchange of goods and services between countries. Exports are goods and services sold to other countries; imports are goods and services bought from other countries. Visible trade is trade in goods that can be seen and counted, such as cocoa or timber. Invisible trade is trade in services such as banking, insurance, shipping and tourism. Trade between two countries is *bilateral*; trade among many countries is *multilateral*. The balance of trade is the value of visible exports minus the value of visible imports. A surplus (favourable balance) means exports are larger; a deficit (unfavourable balance) means imports are larger.

### Why countries trade
Resources, climate and skills are spread unequally among countries. By specialising in what they produce at the lowest cost and trading the surplus, countries obtain more goods, a wider variety, larger markets and new technology.

### Problems and restrictions
Heavy dependence on a few exports can leave a country weak when their prices fall, and cheap imports can harm local firms. *Dumping* is selling goods abroad at a lower price than in the home market. Governments restrict imports with a tariff (a tax on imports), a quota (a limit on quantity), an embargo (a ban) or subsidies to local producers.

### Exchange rate and terms of trade
The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. When a currency appreciates it buys more of another currency: imports become cheaper in that currency and exports become dearer for foreign buyers. Depreciation is the opposite. The terms of trade compare export prices with import prices:

$$\text{Terms of trade} = \frac{\text{index of export prices}}{\text{index of import prices}} \times 100$$

A rise in this figure is an improvement, because the same quantity of exports buys more imports.
sections.formule_principale: $\text{Terms of trade} = \frac{\text{index of export prices}}{\text{index of import prices}} \times 100$

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the command word is define or state and each part carries 2 marks
variantes.contenu_markdown: Write a full sentence that names the thing and says what it is, then add an example. For example, exports are goods and services produced in one country and sold to buyers in other countries, such as cocoa sold abroad.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a rate such as one dollar equals so many FCFA is given
variantes.contenu_markdown: To change a foreign price into FCFA, multiply by the number of FCFA per unit of the foreign currency. To change an FCFA price into foreign currency, divide. If one unit of foreign currency buys fewer FCFA than before, the FCFA has appreciated against it.

variantes.nom: Terms of trade and balance of trade
variantes.quand_utiliser: When two price indices or two values of trade are given
variantes.contenu_markdown: Terms of trade use price indices (export index divided by import index, times 100). Balance of trade uses values (visible exports minus visible imports). Do not mix them.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Suppose that one US dollar was worth 600 FCFA and later became worth 500 FCFA.
(a) State what has happened to the FCFA against the dollar.
(b) Calculate the FCFA price of a machine costing 3,000 dollars before and after the change.
(c) A Cameroonian product sells for 60,000 FCFA. Calculate its price in dollars before and after, and state the effect on Cameroon's exports to the United States.

etapes.action: Compare how many FCFA one dollar buys.
etapes.justification: If a dollar buys fewer FCFA, each FCFA buys more dollars.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The FCFA has **appreciated**, because it now buys more dollars.

etapes.action: Convert the machine's price at the old rate.
etapes.justification: Multiply the dollar price by FCFA per dollar.

etapes.action: Convert the price at the new rate.
Convert the export price into dollars.
etapes.justification: Divide the FCFA price by FCFA per dollar.
A higher dollar price makes the product dearer for American buyers, who may buy less.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Exports to the United States are likely to **fall**.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The FCFA appreciated. Imports priced in dollars became cheaper in FCFA (1,500,000 instead of 1,800,000), but the 60,000 FCFA product became dearer for US buyers (120 dollars instead of 100), so exports are likely to fall.

items.erreur_markdown: "Exports are the goods that a country buys from other countries."
items.pourquoi_faux: This is the definition of imports.
items.correction_markdown: Exports are goods and services sold to other countries; imports are bought from other countries.

items.erreur_markdown: "The price of the dollar rose from 500 to 600 FCFA, so the FCFA has appreciated."
items.pourquoi_faux: A dollar now costs more FCFA, which means each FCFA buys fewer dollars.
items.correction_markdown: The FCFA has depreciated against the dollar. The FCFA appreciates when a dollar costs fewer FCFA.

items.erreur_markdown: "Dumping means throwing away waste in another country."
items.pourquoi_faux: Dumping in economics is about price, not rubbish.
items.correction_markdown: Dumping is selling goods abroad at a price lower than the price in the home market.

items.erreur_markdown: "The terms of trade are the difference between the value of exports and the value of imports."
items.pourquoi_faux: That describes the balance of trade. Terms of trade compare price indices.
items.correction_markdown: Terms of trade $= \frac{\text{export price index}}{\text{import price index}} \times 100$.

items.erreur_markdown: "A tariff is a ban on imports."
items.pourquoi_faux: A ban is an embargo. A tariff only raises the price of imports.
items.correction_markdown: A tariff is a tax on imported goods; a quota limits quantity; an embargo bans trade.

items.enonce_markdown:
Say whether each item is a visible export, an invisible export, a visible import or an invisible import for Cameroon.
(a) A shipment of timber is sold abroad.
(b) A foreign tourist pays for a hotel stay in Kribi.
(c) A Cameroonian company buys lorries from abroad.
(d) A Cameroonian firm pays a foreign insurance company.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Visible export**: a good sold abroad.
(b) **Invisible export**: a service sold to a foreigner, which brings in foreign money.
(c) **Visible import**: a good bought from abroad.
(d) **Invisible import**: a service bought from a foreign firm.

items.enonce_markdown:
In one year a country had visible exports of 4,200 million FCFA and visible imports of 4,900 million FCFA. Its export price index was 108 and its import price index was 120.
(a) Calculate the balance of trade and say whether it is favourable.
(b) Calculate the terms of trade and say whether they improved or worsened.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Balance of trade $= 4\,200 - 4\,900 = -700$ million FCFA: a **deficit of 700 million FCFA**, which is unfavourable.
(b) Terms of trade $= \frac{108}{120} \times 100 = 90$: **90**, below 100, so the terms of trade have **worsened**: the same exports buy fewer imports.

items.enonce_markdown:
Suppose one US dollar was worth 550 FCFA and later became worth 600 FCFA.
(a) State what has happened to the FCFA against the dollar.
(b) A Cameroonian importer buys spare parts costing 2,000 dollars. Calculate the cost in FCFA before and after, and the extra cost.
(c) A US buyer purchases cocoa priced at 1,200,000 FCFA. Calculate its price in dollars after the change, and state whether cocoa exports are encouraged or discouraged.
(d) Give one effect of the change on prices in Cameroon.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) A dollar buys more FCFA, so the FCFA has **depreciated** against the dollar.
(b) Before: $2\,000 \times 550 = 1\,100\,000$ FCFA. After: $2\,000 \times 600 = 1\,200\,000$ FCFA. Extra cost $= 100\,000$ FCFA: **100,000 FCFA more**.
(c) After: $\frac{1\,200\,000}{600} = 2\,000$ dollars. Before it was about $2\,181.8$ dollars. The price in dollars has fallen, so cocoa exports are **encouraged**: **2,000 dollars**.
(d) Imported goods and imported raw materials cost more in FCFA, which can push up prices in Cameroon.

items_markdown: Exports are sold to other countries; imports are bought from them. Visible trade is in goods; invisible trade is in services.
Balance of trade is visible exports minus visible imports; a surplus is favourable and a deficit is unfavourable.
Trade between two countries is bilateral; dumping is selling abroad at a lower price than at home; tariffs, quotas and embargoes restrict imports.
An appreciating currency buys more foreign currency, so imports become cheaper and exports dearer; depreciation does the opposite.
Terms of trade $= \frac{\text{export price index}}{\text{import price index}} \times 100$: above 100 is an improvement, below 100 is a deterioration.
